caseno: Appeal from Original Order No. 81 of 1996 with Civil Rule No. 163(FM) of 1996
lawyer:
AF Hassan Ariff with Borhanuddin, Advocates — For the Appellant
SR Pal with ASM Wahedul Momin Chowdhury, Advocates — For the Respondent Nos.1-6
parties:
Rajdhani Unnayan Kartipakha ------ Appellant
Vs.
Mohammed Jabed Ali and others ------ Respondents
full_judgment:
Mohammad Gholam Rabbani J : Rajdhani Unnayan Kartripakka, briefly, RAJUK along with Government of Bangladesh represented by the Deputy Commissioner, Dhaka, Additional Deputy Commissioner Land Acquisition), Dhaka and (Land Acquisition Officer. Dhaka, are the defendants in Title Suit No.218 of 1994 instituted by the respondent Nos.1-6 in the 3rd Court of Subordinate Judge, Dhaka.

2. Plaint case briefly is this, certain lands owned by the plaintiffs along with the lands of others were requisitioned in LA Case No.138 of 1961-62 on 31-5-62 under the Town Improvement Act of 1953. Initially area of the lands requisitioned was 2760.00 acres, but subsequently in 1966 the area under requisition was reduced to 832.00 acres and consequently Deputy Commissioner, Dhaka, was requested by Rajuk to derequisition the remaining requistioned lands and to order the owners concerned for refunding the compensation money already paid to them. In spite of the said position long thereafter Rajuk published a tender notice being No.3/-94-95 on 22-9-94 in the daily Inqilab inviting tender for filling up the lands left out of the requisition and for this plaintiffs were restrained to file the present suit.

3. In the suit plaintiffs filed an application for temporary injunction praying for staying the operation of the said tender notice so that Rajuk could not fill up the lands in question till the disposal of the suit. By the order dated 18-4-96 learned Subordinate Judge passed an order of temporary injunction to that effect on contest. Hence this appeal by Rajuk

4. Mr AF Hassain Ariff. learned Advocate for the appellant, at the outset submits that the suit is per se barred by res judicata in view of the fact that plaintiffs and others filed writ petitions in the High Court Division against Rajuk in 1992 challenging the publication of a notice on 4-5-92 by Rajuk inviting applications for allotment of the lands in question under the project named Nikunja Residential Area and the writ petitions were discharged rejecting the claim of the petitioner that the lands in question stood released from requisition. Mr. Ariff placed before us a copy of the analogous judgment passed in the writ petitions.

5. It appears that the writ petitions were dismissed on three grounds. One is that the claim of the petitioners as the successors-in-interest of the original owners from whom the lands in question were requisitioned could not be determined without evidence and hence the claim was outside the scope of the writ jurisdiction. Other is that the petitioners were guilty of undue delay and latches in seeking the relief though they were aware that the lands were kept under requisition for a long time. Another is that there is no provision in the Town Improvement Act of 1953 for releasing the property once requisitioned and so the claim that the lands in question stood automatically released or that the same should be released from requisition could not be entertained.

6. It is an admitted fact that the Deputy Commissioner issued instruction on 6-5-66 for releasing the lands in question from requisition on the request of Rajuk and consequently some of the owners of the requisitioned land refunded the compensation money they received and the plaintiffs before us asserted that they also wanted to refund the compensation money but could not. Therefore, the issue before us is not that the plaintiffs are seeking a declaration to the effect that the lands in question was released from requisition, but they are seeking a relief to the effect that Rajuk after a long time and in view of its said intention in 1966 not to use the lands in question is debarred from claiming the lands in 1992.

<u>7. To get an order of temporary injunction for maintaining status quo in respect of the subject-matter of the suit it is only necessary for the person who seeks such an interlocutory order to show firstly that he has got an arguable case and secondly if such an order is not passed then balance of convenience will be disturbed. In 1962 the plaintiffs and other persons got the impression that their lands would not be used by Rajuk. At that time only a part of the compensation money was paid to those persons. After that some of them refunded the money received by them and others could not. But the fact remained that these persons did neither get the opportunity to take any step to regain the loss suffered if it is taken that they lost the lands for ever. So the doctrine of promissory estoppel comes in. Thus we find that the plaintiffs have an arguable case.</u>

8. Mr SR Pal, learned Advocate for the plaintiffs-respondents, submits that the RS Khatians have already been finally published recording the names of the plaintiffs as tenants under the Government in respect of the lands in question. This also indicates that the plaintiffs can invoke the doctrine of estoppel on the basis of the RS Khatians.

9. By the application for temporary injunction plaintiffs are seeking a modest relief of restraining Rajuk from changing the nature and character of the lands in question till the disposal of the suit. We find that the rule of balance of convenience will be satisfied if such an order is passed. We, therefore, find no illegality or irregularity in the impugned order of temporary injunction passed by the trial Court. However, we find that the suit must be disposed of as quickly as possible and the trial Court should not allow any unnecessary adjournment, if prayed for by either of the parties.

10. In the result, this appeal is dismissed without costs. Connected Civil Rule No. 163(fm) of 1996 in discharged without costs.

11. Since I beg to differ with the judgment delivered by my learned brother I would like to deliver a separate judgment in the matter as under.

12. Relevant fact leading to the filing of the present First Miscellaneous Appeal is as follows: The respondent opposite party Nos. 1 to 6 as plaintiffs have instituted Title Suit No. 219 of 1994 in the Court of the 3rd Subordinate Judge, Dhaka, for declaration that as they have right, title, interest in the plaint schedule land, plaint schedule land is no longer included in the LA Case No. 138/61-62 and that the notification No. 3/94-95 dated 22-9-94 published in the Daily Inqilab inviting tender for earth filling is illegal and void.

13. The plaint case of the respondent Nos. 1 to 6, in short, is that land of CS Khatian Nos. 81, 370, 350, 401, 229, 391 and 362 in total about 12.64 acres of land in Mouza boar Sahara originally belonged to Atabuddin and Golapdi, sons of late Doulate Sheikh in 8 annas shares and the same was amicably partitioned between the brothers. The plaintiffs inherited 12.64 acres of land out of CS Khatian No. 350, 401, 229, 2192, 391 and 362. Both SA Khatian and last RS Khatian were also prepared in the name of the present plaintiffs. The aforesaid 12-64 acres of land belonging to the plaintiffs were requisitioned under the said LA Case No. 138/61-62 inclusive of total 2760 acres of land from 11 moujas including Mouza Joar Shahara. The plaintiffs in spite of said requisition are all along in physical possession of the said land by paying rents to the Government. As per decision of the Board of Trustees of the former DIT now RAJUK the Government served notice on 31-5-1962 for requisition of 2760 acres of land including the aforesaid 12-64 acres of land of the plaintiffs vide LA Case No. 138/61-62. The Deputy Commissioner. Dhaka fixed a preliminary compensation for the land at the rate of Taka 8,952.75 and Taka 10,288.19 respectively and paid small amount to the predecessor of the plaintiffs at the rate of Taka 4,580.00 and Taka 8,000.00 as against actual current rate of Taka 5 (five) lakh per katha by way of compensation. Subsequently the Board of Trustees of former DIT now RAJUK took the decision in the meeting held on 15-12-1965 to acquire only 832 acres of land out of the said 2760 acres of land as the implementation of the scheme for such a vast area was impracticable and accordingly, requested the Deputy Commissioner, Dhaka to release the rest of the land from requisition. Accordingly, the Ministry of land Administration directed the Deputy Commissioner, Dhaka on 6-5-1966 to take steps for derequisition of the said excess land and to ask for refund of the compensation money. The predecessor of the plaintiffs received such notice of derequisition and refund on 6-9-1966 and wanted to refund the compensation money received by them but could not succeed.

14. In this background of the matter the plaintiffs asserted that their land was in fact derequisitioned and, as such, the notification published in the Daily Inquilab by the appellant i.e. Rajuk for earth filing of their lands was illegal and void.

15. The plaintiffs also filed an application under Order 39 rule 2 read with section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure for restraining the defendant No.3 RAJUK ie the appellant from earth filling the suit land contending, inter alia, that the implementation of the said notification will create disturbance in the peaceful possession of the plaintiffs in their land in question. The defendant No. 3 ie the appellant RAJUK filed written objection denying all the material allegations asserting that the suit schedule lands were requisitioned long ago vide LA Case No. 138/61-62 and RAJUK obtained delivery of possession of the said land as contemplated under section 93A(3) of the Town Improvement Act, 1953 for the purpose of development of the said land and the plaintiffs have no right, title and interest as well as possession in the suit schedule land.

16. The trial Court by the impugned judgment and order granted an order of temporary injunction against RAJUK. Hence RAJUK filed this First Miscellaneous Appeal challenging the impugned order of temporary injunction and obtained the order of status quo.

17. Mr AF Hassan Ariff, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the appellant, submits that the suit schedule land together with other land was requisitioned by RAJUK for the development of greater Dhaka and since the said scheme was approved by the Government and is being executed phase by phase and the present project "Nikunja Residential Area" is within the said scheme RAJUK should not be debarred from developing and utilising the said land for the said project which is a public purpose. The learned Advocate further contends that the plaintiffs previously filed Writ Petition No. 3734 of 1992 challenging the notification for allotment of the said land on the ground that the said land was, in fact, derequisitioned. But a Division Bench of the High Court Division by the judgment dated 22-11-1993 rejected the said Writ Petition along with other similar Writ Petitions filed by other land owners affected by the said LA Case being Writ Petition Nos. 3078 of 1992 and 3733 of 1992 and the plaintiffs thereafter challenged the said judgment before the Appellate Division by filing Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal Nos. 117-120/1994. The Appellate Division also rejected the aforesaid leave petitions and affirmed the said judgment of High Court Division holding that the land in question was never derequisitioned and the RAJUK was in possession of the same. The learned Advocate therefore submits that the prayer for injunction in this background of the matter is not at all maintainable.

18. Mr SR Pal, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the respondents, on the other hand, contends that since the government decided to implement the development scheme covering an area of only 832 acres of land or so and also directed the owners of the land failling out side of the said 832 acres of land to refund the compensation money, if so received by them, such land falling outside of the said 832 acres of land stood derequisitioned and as such the impugned notification for earth filing of such land after about 30 years of requisition is illegal and without jurisdiction. Mr SR Pal also contends by producing a RS Khatian that the said khatian also shows that the plaintiffs are in possession of the same and, as such, the plaintiffs have good prima facie arguable case for injunction.

19. We have heard the learned Advocates of both the sides and perused the judgment dated 22-11-1993 passed by a Division Bench of the High Court Division in Writ Petition No. 3734 of 1992. The said Division Bench of the High Court Division in the aforesaid judgment on careful consideration of the facts and law involved in the case categorically found that the land requisitioned in LA Case No. 138/61-62 was validly requisitioned and the former DIT now Rajuk obtained delivery of possession of the land involved therein which included plaint schedule land and the requisition not having been challenged by the owners of the land the land falling outside 832 acres of land never stood derequsitioned. Moreso, when there is no provision for derequisition in the Town Improvement Act. 1953. It is further held in the said judgment that since Nikunza Residential Area is a part of the main scheme for development of greater Dhaka Rajuk can use and deal with the same as may appear to be expedient.

<u>20. Since the Division Bench of the High Court Division by the said judgment in Writ Petition No. 3734 of 1992 held that the land in question was never derequisitioned and RAJUK was entitled to deal with it phase by phase and since the said judgment was affirmed by the Appellate Division, plaintiffs-respondent''s claim for injunction in respect of the said land appears to be not maintainable in law. Hence the finding of the trial Court that plaintiffs-respondents have prima facie case for injunction is erratic and perverse.</u>

21. In that view of the matter I am inclined to allow the appeal and set aside the impugned judgment and order. Hence this appeal is allowed without costs. Impugned judgment and order dated 18-4-1996 in Title Suit No. 218 of 1994 passed by the learned Subordinate Judge. 3rd Court, Dhaka, is set aside.

Connected Rule is accordingly disposed of.

Order

Since we have differed, let the record be placed before the learned Chief Justice. We have differed regarding the issue as to whether the instant suit is barred by res judicata in view of the judgment and order dated 22-11-93 passed in Writ Petition No. 3734 of 1992.

End.

Kazi Ebadul Hoque J

Appeal from Original Order No. 81 of 1996

With

Civil Rule No. 163 (fm) of 1996

Rajdhani Unnayan Karti-pakha ------ Appellant

Vs.

Mohammed Jabed Ali and others ------ Respondents

Judgment June 19th, 1997

AF Hassan Ariff with Borhanuddin, Advocates -------- For the Appellant

SR Paul with ASM Wahedul Momin Chowdhury, Advocates ------- For the Respondents

Judgment

Kazi Ebadul Hoque J: This appeal has been sent to me by the learned Chief Justice as the Division Bench which heard the appeal differed equally in their opinion regarding the issue as to whether the suit is barred by res judicata in view of the judgment and order dated 22-11-93 passed in Writ Petition No.3734 of 1992.

<u>24. Proviso to sub-section (2) of section 98 of the Code of Civil Procedure provides that where the Bench hearing the appeal composed of two judges differ in their opinion on point of law, they may state the point of law upon which they differ and the appeal then shall be heard upon that point only by one or more of the other Judges of the Court, and such point shall be decided according to the opinion of the majority of such Judges. In the case of Brindaban Chandra vs. Mst. Rezia Begum reported in 16 DLR 77 Murshed J (as his Lordship then was) considered the scope of a reference to a Judge for deciding an appeal after difference of opinion between the two Judges composing the Division Bench under clause 36 of the Letters Patent of 1865 of the Calcutta High Court which was applicable to the then Dhaka High Court and section 98 of the Code of Civil Procedure. His Lordship noticed that by virtue of sub-section (3) of the said section 98 provisions of clause 36 of the Letters Patent would prevail. Under the provisions of the Laws Continuance Enforcement Order of the 10th April 1971 aforesaid Letters Patent continued to be in force and under the provisions of Article 149 of the Constitution of the People''s Republic of Bangladesh aforesaid Letters Patent continued as the existing law till its repeal by the provisions of section 3 of Law Reforms Ordinance 1978 and, as such, the said sub-section (3) of section 98 has become nugatory. So I have to decide the aforesaid question only on which my learned brothers differed.</u>

25. Learned Advocate for the appellant submitted that in the judgment dated 22-11-93 of the High Court Division passed in Writ Petition No. 3734 of 1992 as upheld by the Appellate Division by its judgment dated 27-3-94 in Civil Petition Nos. 117-119/1994 it was held that the suit land is still under requisition and RAJUK may deal with the said land as it appears expedient to RAJUK and, as such, plaintiff''s prayers in the Title Suit No.218/1994 for declaration that suit land was not under requisition in LA Case No.138/61-62 and defendant No. 3 RAJUK''s tender notice for filling up the suit land was illegal and that the plaintiffs have title in the suit land are nothing but reagitating the self same question agitated in the aforesaid writ petition. He contended that in the writ petition the question as to whether the suit land was under requisition having been finally declined on merit plaintiffs cannot raise the self same question in the suit again and such claim is barred by the principle of res judicata and so the plaintiffs are not entitled to temporary injunction. He further submitted that under the provisions of section 93C of the Town Improvement Act plaintiffs suit challenging the requisition is wholly barred and on that ground also plaintiffs'' suit is not maintainable and, as such, trial Court was not justified in holding that the suit is maintainable and allowing plaintiffs'' prayer for temporary injunction.

26. Learned Advocate for the plaintiff-respondents submitted that res judicata is a question of maintainability for the suit and that cannot be decided in granting temporary injunction. If the Court finds that plaintiffs have an arguable prima facie case and would suffer irreparable loss and balance of conveniences and inconveniences is also in favour of the plaintiffs then Court is to grant temporary injunction. He further contended that decision in the writ petition cannot operate as res judicata in a suit between the same parties and, as such, the decision of the High Court Division in the aforesaid writ petition as affirmed by the Appellate Division cannot be a bar to the granting of temporary injunction by the Court in favour of the plaintiff respondents. So, the order of temporary injunction granted by the trial Court suffers from no illegality.

27. Before deciding the question whether the suit is barred by res judicata let me consider the objection raised by the learned Advocate of the respondents that res judicata is a question of maintainability of the suit and that cannot be considered in deciding temporary injunction matter.

28. In the case of Mansur Ahmed vs. Kalipada reported in 11 DLR 103 it has been held:

"Whether for want of notice under section 80 CPC the suit is maintainable or not, it is a question to be decided in the suit. The Court in considering the question of temporary injunction cannot prejudge the maintainability of the suit. It is not necessary for the plaintiff, for temporary injunction, to establish, that he had got a good prima facie case which is likely to be decreed. If the plaintiff has got an arguable case, that is enough for the purpose of temporary injunction. So far as the injunction is concerned, he is to prove a prima facie case for injunction. No court should go into merit of the suit in which temporary injunction is prayed for."

29. In the case of Mian Md Latif vs. Province of West Pakistan reported in PLD 1970 (SC) 180: 22 DLR SC 98 it has been held:

"The allegation of the appellant is that the impugned certificate for various reasons mentioned above is nullity in the eye of law and has not been passed in accordance with the provision of the relevant law. On the above principle civil Courts have jurisdiction to examine these questions. We would therefore, hold that the learned Courts below, in these circumstances were not justified in holding that the appellant''s suit was not competent. The plaintiff has only to make out that he has a good prima facie case and he will suffer irreparable injury."

30. In the case of Dhaka Match Factory Ltd. vs. Bangladesh Match Co. Ltd. reported in 30 DLR 244 it has been held:

"It is clear that on the question of maintainability the suit ought not to have been rejected as at the time of hearing of the application for temporary injunction there was insufficient evidence before Court for arriving at a correct decision in the matter. The facts of the case reported in DLR 10 have hardly got any relevance it the instant case."

31. In the case of Jamalpur Fisheries Co-operative Society Ltd. vs. DC Kishoregonj reported in 47 DLR 573 it has been held:

"Apart from that in deciding the matter of temporary injunction upon an application under Order 39 rules 1 and 2 of the Code of Civil Procedure. maintainability of the suit should not be gone into and properly decided particularly when there will be necessity of evidence at the trial of the suit for correctly deciding such issue. The present suit is not of such a nature where without any evidence it can be correctly decided, at this stage that the suit is barred by any law."

32. From the above decision it appears that maintainability should be decided at the trial after taking evidence and not at the interlocutory stage of hearing temporary injunction matter.

33. On the other hand, in the case of Shamsuddin Khan vs. Shamsuzzaman reported in 22 DLR 655 it has been observed:

"It is true that if a suit itself is not maintainable and if the Court has no jurisdiction to entertain the suit the Court neither gives the final decision nor the interlocutory decision in the matter.

34. In the case of Choumuhani College vs. Ismail Hossain reported in 26 DLR 10 it has been held:

"If on a mere reading of the plaint it is found that the suit is not maintainable the Court has to decide the said point even when it is called upon to consider the question of issuing a temporary injunction."

35. In that case temporary injunction granted by the Courts below was set aside holding that the suit was not maintainable on the decision in the case of Burmah Eastern Ltd. vs. Burmah Eastern Employees Union reported in 18 DLR 709. In that case Murshed CJ observed that.

"a still born suit should be properly buried, at its inception, so that no further time is consumed on a fruitless litigation".

36. Similarly, in the case of Marghub Siddique vs. Hamid Ali reported in 1974  SCMR 519 it has been observed.

"An injunction is not to be granted on the basis that a prima facie case exists, but it is incumbent upon the Court to take into account the other questions."

37. In the case of Nur Mohammad vs. Mvi. Moinuddin Ahmed reported in 1986 BLD (AD), 342 Appellate Division while deciding the question whether plaint was liable to be rejected in view of the bar under section 14A of the (Emergency) Requisition of Property Act, 1948 at the time of hearing injunction matter held disagreeing with the aforesaid decision of the Pakistan Supreme Court in Mian Md. Latif''s case:

"In our opinion section 14A of the (Emergency) Requisition of Property Act has in clear and unmistakable terms, put an express embargo on entertainment of any suit or application against any order or action under the Act."

38. In that case Appellate Division further observed. "A Judge may have sympathy for a litigant suffering due to technicalities of law made by the legislature, still in view of the express legislative intention he must follow the "hands off doctrine." Otherwise chaos and anomaly would prevail leading to all sorts of complications and confusion. Whatever the legislature says, unless it is contrary to the constitution, its mandate, either express or implied, has been obeyed by Court. "it may be mentioned that similar bar has been imposed under the provisions of section 93C of the Town Improvement Act which is as follows :"Bar to Jurisdiction of Civil Court : Except as expressly provided in this Chapter, no civil Court shall entertain any suit or application against any order passed or any action taken under this Chapter and all suits and appeals pending in any such Court against any such order passed or any action taken under this Chapter shall abate with effect from the date of coming into force of the Town Improvement (Amendment) Ordinance, 1965."

But in the instant case no objection was raised before the Court below, or Division Bench on the ground that the suit is barred under the aforesaid provision. So I need not decide such a point specially when such question is beyond the refeence made to me.

<u>39. Thus, on consideration of the above decision it is clear that question of maintainability of the suit cannot be decided at the interlocutory stage of hearing temporary injunction matter when evidence would be required to decide the same. But such question can be decided at that stage when from the averments made in the plaint or from admitted facts apparent on the face of the record it appears that the suit is expressly or impliedly barred by or under any law or the suit is not otherwise maintainable. In such circumstances decision on the question of maintainability of the suit need not be postponed till the trial of the suit in considering prayer for temporary injunction in a case where there is no necessity of taking evidence for deciding such a question.</u>

40. Let me see whether the suit is barred by the principle of res judicata on the averments made in the plaint or on admitted facts or whether it is a disputed question to be decided after taking evidence at the trial of the suit.

41. In the instant case admittedly suit land has been requisitioned under the now repealed provisions of section 93A of the Town Improvement Act 1953 and the plaintiffs filed Writ Petition No.3734 of 1992 and by judgment dated 22-11-93 Rule was discharged by a Division Bench of the High Court Division and the aforesaid Judgment of the High Court Division was upheld by the Appellate Division by its judgment dated 27-3-94 passed in Civil Petition for Special Leave to Appeal Nos.117-119 of 1994. If on reading the aforesaid judgments between the same parties in respect of the self same land and averments made in the plaint the question of maintainability of the suit can be decided then there can be no objection to deciding same on the ground that maintainability cannot be decided before trial of the suit.

42. It appears from the plaint that plaintiffs prayed for declaration of their title in the suit land by inheritance, declaration that the suit land is not included under the notice of requisition in LA Case No.138/61-62 and that tender notice issued by the defendant No.3 in the daily Inqilab to engage contractors for filling up the suit land is without jurisdiction and void in respect of the suit land. In the plaint plaintiffs alleged that their title in the suit land has been clouded by the defendants'' action in not releasing the suit land twenty years after issuing the de-requisition notice and by the tender notice published in the daily Inqilab on 22-9-94 for filling up the suit land. There is no allegation in the plaint that plaintiffs'' title to get compensation money in respect of the suit requisitioned and has been denied by the defendants. If the entire plaint is read it is clear that the plaintiffs having claimed that though their predecessor could not refund the compensation money in pursuance of a notice of de-requisition their land is not under requisition and, as such, they are entitled to declaration of their title in the suit land and further declaration that their land is not under requisition in the aforesaid Land Acquisition Case and, as such, defendant No. 3 cannot ask any contractor to fill up the suit land with earth.

43. It appears from the judgment of the Writ Petition No. 3734 of 1992 dated 22-11-92 that the High Court Division negatived plaintiffs'' claim that the suit land is no longer under requisition and further held that RAJUK is entitled to use or deal with the land as it appears to it expedient under the provisions of section 92A(3) of the Act. Appellate Division while affirming the aforesaid judgment of the High Court Division observed that "the various resolutions taken by the Board of Trustees of the former DIT reducing from time to time the quantum of land to be acquired have neither attained any statutory force nor been implemented by refund of the compensation money" and, as such, "the order of requisition under section 93A made in the sixties cannot be made null and void on such facts."

44. From the above it is clear that plaintiffs as petitioners in the writ petition claimed that though the suit land was requisitioned for the DIT predecessor of the defendant No. 3 RAJUK in the aforesaid LA Case and compensation money was paid to their predecessor, he could not refund the same in spite of notice for de-requisition of the land and, as such, the land was not under requisition. But such claim of the plaintiffs was negatived by the High Court Division as well as the Appellate Division clearly holding that the suit land is under requisition. In the Title Suit No. 281/1994 plaintiffs again claimed that the suit land is not under requisition and agitating the very same question agitated in the aforesaid Writ Petition. In such circumstances it is to be seen whether the suit is barred by the principles of res judicata.

45. In the case of Joseph vs. State of Kerala reported in 1965 (SC) 1514 Supreme Court of India held "If by a final decision of a competent Court his title to property has been negatived, he ceased to have the fundamental right in respect of that property and therefore, he can no longer enforce it. In that context the doctrine of res judicata may be invoked." But the Supreme Court did not apply the principle of res judicata in that case as the earlier Writ Petition filed by the petitioner was not dismissed on merit but on preliminary question of maintainability.

46. In the case of Mohammad Chiragh Uddin Bhatti vs. Province of West Pakistan n reported in 1971 SCMR 447 Supreme Court of Pakistan held "Even if section 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure may not in terms apply in support of the plea of res judicata it can hardly be disputed that the general principle of res judicata were clearly attracted to debar the petitioner from negotiating the matter afresh by a civil suit, which have been put at rest by a judgment of the High Court passed in Writ Jurisdiction."

47. In the case of Union of India vs. Nanak Singh reported in AIR 1968 (SC) 1970 it has been held that decision of the High Court in a writ petition negativing claim of the petitioner that authority terminating him from service was not competent to do so shall operate as res judicata in the subsequent suit filed by the petitioner for declaration that his termination was by an authority lower in rank than competent to pass such order.

48. From the above decisions it is clear that a question decided in a writ petition disposed of on merit cannot be reagitated in a subsequent suit between the same parties on the principle of res judicata.

49. In the instant case plaintiff respondents are reagitating the very same question agitated in the writ petition filed by them against the defendant appellants though the question has been set at rest by the decision in the writ petition disposed of on merit and affirmed by the Appellate Division. Even the plaintiffs cannot raise the very same question invoking the doctrine of promissory estoppel which is also barred by the principle of constructive res judicata. Moreover, there is no averment in the plaint that the defendants are estoppel from claiming the suit land as requisitioned land under the doctrine of promissory estoppel. No such plea was raised in the plaint.

50. In view of the above I find no merit in the contention of the learned Advocate for the respondent that decision in the aforesaid writ petition filed by the plaintiffs will not debar them from reagitating the same question in the suit filed by them against the defendant appellants.

51. Learned Advocate for the respondents brought to my notice order dated 31-7-95 passed by the Subordinate Judge in the said Title Suit No. 218 of 1994 rejecting prayer of the appellants for rejecting of the plaint under Order 7 rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure on the ground that decision in the writ petition will not be a bar to proceed with the suit and submitted that the appellants having not challenged, the said order before the Higher Court they cannot reagitate the question of res judicata in this appeal. Learned Advocate for the appellants could not say what steps his clients took against the said order. In such circumstances contention of the learned Advocate for the respondents that the appellants did not take any step for setting aside that order has force.

52. In this appeal question is not that the suit being barred by the principle of res judicata the plaint should be rejected. The question is, whether the plaintiffs are entitled to the prayer for temporary injunction if the suit is not prima facie maintainable being barred by the principle of res judicata. In that view of the matter I am of the opinion that there can be no objection in deciding such a question in this appeal specially when no such objection was taken earlier before the Court below or the Division Bench which differed only on this question.

53. In the above facts and circumstances and discussions made above I am of the view that the suit filed by the plaintiff respondent is barred by the principles of res judicata. I am, therefore, of the opinion in agreement with my learned brother Md Joynal Abedin, J that in view of the decision of the High Court Division in Writ Petition No. 3734 of 1992 as affirmed by the Appellate Division plaintiff respondents'' claim for temporary injunction in respect of the suit land is not maintainable. I am therefore of the view that the appeal should be allowed.

In the result, the appeal is allowed without cost as directed by Md Joynal Abedin J and the impugned judgment and order of the Court below dated 18-4-96 is set aside and the connected Rule is disposed of accordingly.

End.
